headline: AUD weakness near 70 cents is a US dollar story, with markets now pricing up to four more Fed hikes — a complete reversal from start-of-year expectations
reasoning: Dr Rynne attributes the Australian dollar's difficulty staying above 70 cents primarily to US dollar strength rather than domestic weakness. Markets in the US have repriced to expect up to four additional 25 basis point increases in the federal funds rate, a dramatic turnaround from the rate-cut expectations that prevailed at the beginning of the year, which is driving broad USD appreciation.

So the fact now is that the markets in the US are pricing in um, are up to full 25 basis point increases in the federal funds rate, which is, um, you know, complete reversal of where it's all, uh, where we saw rates were going to go. headline: Households scrambling for work as cost-of-living pressures bite; participation rate near record high signals financial stress, not strength
reasoning: The participation rate rising to 67.1%, just 0.1% below its peak, is interpreted not as a positive sign but as households being forced into the labour market to maintain income amid rising petrol prices and anticipated higher mortgage repayments. Dr Rynne expects 25–50 basis points of further RBA hikes by year end to add to household pressure. He distinguishes household-driven inflation from government-spending-driven demand, noting household consumption remains roughly 2 percentage points below its pre-COVID trend while government spending is about 4% of GDP higher than its long-run average.
quote: The participation rate has gone up to 67.1%, um, which is just 0.1 of a percent below the peak rate of 67.2, which shows that households are now starting to scramble to look for employment opportunities to keep their income coming in as the cost of living pressures continue to bike with higher petrol prices, but also in anticipation of higher mortgage payments as well. With the impending 25 basis points, possibly 50 basis point rise by the end of the year as well.

headline: Labour market weakness emerging but August jobs data distorted by ABS census hiring of ~30,000 temporary workers; employers retaining flexibility via part-time hiring
reasoning: August employment figures showed 45,000 new jobs created, all in part-time roles, while full-time employment fell by 6,000. Dr Rynne cautions that roughly 30,000 of those part-time jobs were temporary ABS census workers, meaning the true underlying picture is unclear until next month's data. He interprets the shift toward part-time hiring as employers preserving flexibility ahead of a potential economic slowdown.
quote: I think the data showed that there is a weakness, um, that's, uh, emerging more strongly now in the economy. But, uh, what you saw with that was all the employment growth was in part time employment. About 45,000 new jobs were created in August, uh, and full time employment fell by 6000. Now, I think it's a little bit difficult to interpret the last month's data simply because also in August you had the ABS itself employing 30,000 people to do the census. Uh, and so I think we really need to wait and see what happens with next month's data to see how much of that, um, 45,000, uh, of new part time employment is maintained and how much is just in fact casual or temporary to, in fact, do the census itself.

headline: RBA rate hike fully priced in for the next meeting, with possibly another in November; RBA may have erred by not hiking in August
reasoning: Dr Rynne believes a rate hike is locked in at the next RBA meeting and that a second hike in November is also possible. He suggests the RBA will look back regretfully at its decision not to raise rates in August. The August labour force data, while showing some weakness, is complicated by the ABS hiring approximately 30,000 temporary workers for the census, making it difficult to draw firm conclusions about underlying labour market momentum until the next month's data is available.
quote: I think it's fully priced in at the moment. Um, we have, in fact anticipated one in August and as the month progressed, uh, you know, the, the pricing for that fell away. Now, I think in hindsight, the RBA is going to kick themselves. The fact that they didn't increase in August. headline: Aggregate demand being driven by government spending running ~4% of GDP above its long-run average, not by households
reasoning: Dr Rynne notes that the long-run trend in household consumption is currently about 2 percentage points below pre-COVID levels, while government consumption is approximately 4% of GDP above its historical average. This means the elevated aggregate demand driving inflation is primarily a fiscal, not a consumer, phenomenon, supporting the view that hiking rates to suppress household demand is a blunt instrument.
quote: The other thing to recognise is that aggregate demand is really being driven by higher government consumption. So what you can see is that the long term trend of household consumption is about two percentage points less, um, today than that long run trend prior to Covid, but government spending is about 4% higher as a percentage of GDP than what it was over the long run as well. So that higher levels of total aggregate demand in terms of consumption expenditure is really being driven by that 2% delta being caused by much higher levels of government spending.
